details:
**The Tale of Genji**
An early-11th-century work by Lady Murasaki Shikibu, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court in what is now Kyoto. It is often called the world's first novel. It follows Hikaru Genji, the "Shining Prince," an emperor's son who is removed from the line of succession and made a commoner, and his many love affairs with women such as Lady Fujitsubo, his wife Lady Aoi (who dies after giving birth to his son), the Akashi Lady, and "Cicada Shell" (Utsusemi). Genji's death is marked only by a blank chapter titled "Vanished into the Clouds."

**The Pillow Book**
A collection of observations, anecdotes, and lists by Sei Shonagon, a lady-in-waiting at the Heian court around the year 1000. Its famous lists include "Hateful Things" (such as a man beating oxen), "Adorable Things" (such as a child's face drawn on a melon), "Things That Should Be Large" (such as houses and men's eyes), and "Things That Give an Unclean Feeling."

**"Rashomon"**
A 1915 short story by Ryunosuke Akutagawa, set at a ruined gate in old Kyoto. A dismissed servant finds an old woman pulling the hair from corpses to make wigs, and she justifies this by saying the dead woman used to sell snake meat as dried fish. Deciding "I'd starve if I didn't," the servant steals the old woman's clothes and flees. Japan's top prize for new writers, the Akutagawa Prize, is named after him; his other works include the late story "Cogwheels," in which the narrator keeps seeing a man in a raincoat.

**"In a Grove"**
An Akutagawa story about the death of the samurai Takehiro, whose body is found in a forest. A woodcutter, a priest, the bandit Tajomaru, the samurai's wife (whom the bandit raped), and the dead man himself (speaking through a medium) all give contradictory accounts. Akira Kurosawa combined it with "Rashomon" in his 1950 film Rashomon.

**"The Spider's Thread"**
An Akutagawa story in which the Buddha looks down through a lotus pond in paradise and sees the sinner Kandata in hell. Because Kandata once spared a spider, the Buddha lowers a spider's thread for him to climb out of hell's Pool of Blood. When Kandata shouts at the other sinners climbing behind him to get off, the thread snaps and he falls back.

**The Temple of the Golden Pavilion**
Yukio Mishima's 1956 novel, based on the real 1950 arson of Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto. The stuttering acolyte Mizoguchi becomes obsessed with the temple's beauty and remembers the Zen saying "When you meet the Buddha, kill the Buddha." He buys arsenic and a knife, burns the temple down, and then throws them away, deciding that he wants to live.

**The Sea of Fertility**
Mishima's final tetralogy: Spring Snow, Runaway Horses, The Temple of Dawn, and The Decay of the Angel. Shigekuni Honda goes from law student to retired judge while following what seem to be reincarnations of his friend Kiyoaki Matsugae, and in the last book he adopts a boy he believes is the latest reincarnation. Mishima, who also wrote Confessions of a Mask, committed seppuku in 1970 after a failed coup attempt.

**A Personal Matter**
Kenzaburo Oe's 1964 novel about Bird, an alcoholic cram-school English teacher who dreams of going to Africa. His son is born with what looks like a brain hernia, and Bird considers letting the baby die before agreeing to surgery, which shows the condition is less serious than feared. Oe's own son Hikari was born with brain damage, and children with mental disabilities appear often in his fiction.

**Nip the Buds, Shoot the Kids**
Oe's first novel (1958). During World War II, a group of reformatory boys are left in a mountain village when plague breaks out and the villagers flee. Joined by others, including a Korean boy and an army deserter, they build their own community, and the narrator cares for a girl they find hiding in a storehouse. Oe also wrote The Silent Cry, in which a brother sells the family's storehouse to a Korean supermarket owner called "the Emperor."

**"The Dancing Girl of Izu"**
Yasunari Kawabata's 1926 story about a student traveling on the Izu Peninsula with a troupe of traveling performers. He is drawn to the young drummer girl and listens for the sound of her drum, then laughs with relief when she runs out naked from a bathhouse and waves, revealing that she is only a child of about 14. Kawabata also wrote very short "Palm-of-the-Hand" stories, such as "The Grasshopper and the Bell Cricket," in which children with paper lanterns search for insects.

**Snow Country**
Kawabata's novel set in a hot-spring town in Japan's snowy west. The wealthy dilettante Shimamura says his index finger remembers the geisha Komako, who lives at her music teacher's house and practices the shamisen. Kawabata, who won the 1968 Nobel Prize, also wrote The Master of Go, a fictionalized account of the retirement game of the Go master Shusai, narrated by a journalist; and The Sound of the Mountain, in which the aging Shingo forgets how to tie his tie and hears a sound he takes as an omen of death.

**Haruki Murakami**
A contemporary novelist known for jazz records, cats, and dreamlike plots. In Norwegian Wood, Toru Watanabe lands in Hamburg, hears a cover of the Beatles song, and remembers Naoko and her talk of a "field well"; the lively Midori is his other love interest. In 1Q84, Tengo rewrites Fuka-Eri's novel Air Chrysalis. His other novels include The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle.

**Matsuo Basho**
The Edo-period master of haiku, which grew out of the opening verse of renga, a linked poem written by several poets together. His most famous haiku describes a frog jumping into an old pond, and another describes the rough sea stretching out toward Sado Island. He wrote the travel diary The Narrow Road to the Deep North (also translated The Narrow Road to the Interior) and the early collection The Seashell Game.

**Noh, kabuki, and bunraku**
Japan's traditional theater forms. Noh was developed by Kan'ami and his son Zeami, and it follows the pacing principle jo-ha-kyu ("beginning, breaking, rapid"); a traditional noh program has five plays, with comic kyogen pieces in between. Bunraku is puppet theater accompanied by joruri chanting, famous for Chikamatsu Monzaemon's love-suicide plays. Kabuki is known for its stylized acting and bright white makeup.

**I Am a Cat**
Natsume Soseki's satirical novel (1905–1906), narrated by a pompous, nameless house cat. The cat mocks his owner, the schoolteacher Mr. Sneaze (Kushami), and his intellectual friends.
